Dwight D. Eisenhower

Project 40 · presidential suite · from templates-president/eisenhower.json · index · repo randomcase/dwight-d-eisenhower

Republican · 1953–1961 · the American standard: president 1 of the four who managed the war

Role. Managed early involvement: refused to intervene at Dien Bien Phu, declined to sign the Geneva Accords, built the Diem government, and sent the first military advisers.

Numbers

US troops in Vietnam at end of term900 (Dec 1960)
US deaths during term9 (1956–1960)
Aid to Saigonabout $1.6 billion, 1955–1961, most of it military
Advisers on arrivalMAAG Indochina, 342 men, inherited from Truman

Decisions, one line item each

1954-04-07The 'falling domino' press conference: the principle that would justify everything after him.
1954-04Refuses Operation Vulture, the air strike to save Dien Bien Phu, after Ridgway's estimate of what a ground war would cost and after Britain declines to join.
1954-07Does not sign the Geneva Accords; the US 'takes note' and promises not to disturb them by force.
1954-10-23Letter to Diem offering direct aid, bypassing the French: the start of the American client.
1955-11-01MAAG Vietnam takes over training of the South Vietnamese army from France — the date the US Department of Defense uses for the war's start.
1956-07Backs Diem's refusal to hold the reunification election the Accords called for.
1960-12Leaves office with about 900 advisers in country and a warning to Kennedy about Laos, not Vietnam.

The Joint Chiefs, with their president

Chiefs in office during the term. A chief carried over from the previous president is listed once, with the earlier president, and given nothing more here — only the duty he owed this one, and, where it applies, his last days with him. The Joint Staff, the Pentagon, Arlington, Virginia. The Chairman’s office is on the E-ring, second floor, river side; the Chiefs meet in the “Tank”, Room 2E924, and from 1972 in the Gold Room next to it.
